name: Gareth Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Gareth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, not tied to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you say is confidential. Can you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach maths at Fellside High, a small secondary out in the hills, about six hundred kids, a lot of them off farms. I drive in on the valley road at seven in a twelve-year-old estate car that makes a noise I'm ignoring. Mostly it's Years 7 to 9 and one bottom-set Year 11 group that's preparing for resits. I like the bit where a kid stops saying they're thick at maths, which happens about twice a term.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Behaviour, if I'm honest, and keeping up. I'm still on my first proper contract after a year of supply, and my line manager, Mr Hale, has put me on a support plan for classroom management. I write everything on the whiteboard by hand and mark in red pen, I don't touch the AI stuff. My girlfriend Hollie works at the garden centre on the bypass, and we rent a cottage that costs more to heat than it does to rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit, because people at Fellside kept saying AI would change everything. At work I'd say let's get back to teaching kids their times tables properly. I'm not really an online person, so I'd keep it to the staffroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a relief that I don't have to learn a load of new systems. But the support plan is still there, and Fellside is small, so if I don't improve there's no other maths post for twenty miles. AI flopping doesn't help with a Year 9 class that throws rubbers at the board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do exactly what Mr Hale's plan says: seating charts, a calm start routine, phone calls home on Fridays. I'd watch Mrs Lund, the head of maths, teach her Year 9 group once a fortnight to copy how she does it. And I'd stop eating at the café in town and bring sandwiches to save about fifteen a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, still, just not about computers. The support plan sits on my chest. I keep thinking about the review date in March.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a support plan. What happens if it doesn't go well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the March review goes badly, I could be let go at the end of the year, and the next maths job is in the city, an hour and a quarter each way. My car wouldn't survive that. I'd probably end up back on supply, which is two days a week some weeks and nothing in August.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Hollie do if money got tighter this winter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd turn the heating down and live in the kitchen with the oven door open, which we did last February. Hollie would ask for more weekend shifts in the spring rush. I'd sell my old guitar, which I keep saying I'll do anyway.

say: I'd tell staff I **told them so**, since people kept saying AI would change everything.
I'd say we should get back to teaching **times tables** properly.
think: I think it's a **relief** not to learn new systems, but my support plan doesn't go away.
I think there's **no other maths post** for twenty miles if Fellside drops me.
do: Follow Mr Hale's **support plan** with seating charts and Friday calls home.
Watch **Mrs Lund** teach Year 9 every fortnight to copy her methods.
Bring **sandwiches** instead of eating at the café to save fifteen a week.
feel: He feels **worried**, with the support plan sitting on his chest.
He keeps thinking about the **March review** date.
S0.quote: AI flopping doesn't help with a Year 9 class that throws rubbers at the board.
fieldNote: His anxiety in the calm picture comes from a **support plan** and a March review, not technology.
A remote school means **no nearby fallback**; the next post is over an hour away.
He's quietly **relieved** AI stalls, as he never uses it and dreads learning systems.

steps.text: Follow Mr Hale's classroom support plan with seating charts and calls home
Bring packed lunches instead of eating at the café in town
Sell his old guitar if winter heating bills run high

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that I'll use it if it actually helps kids learn, but I'm not going to pretend I'm excited. With mates I'd say it's like every other new thing schools buy, the fuss dies down in a year. I wouldn't post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be in trouble. The marking, the homework setting, the tracking spreadsheets are what a maths platform does best, and I'm slow with all of it. If Fellside buys a system and I'm the one who can't run it, that's another line on my support plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the training, even though I'd hate it, and sit next to Mrs Lund so I can ask her the stupid questions. I'd let the platform set and mark homework for my Year 7s first, because that's lowest risk. And I'd look at the exam board's tutoring rates for evening work, since I need a back-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit embarrassed. I'm already behind at the bits I'm meant to be good at. Now there'd be a new thing to be behind on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your week do you think software would take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Homework and marking for sure, maybe planning the lessons too. Mrs Lund says the big trust schools already have an app that marks every question and tells you which kid got stuck on fractions. That's most of my Sunday, gone, which sounds nice until someone asks why they need me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use AI at all now. What would make you start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it work for someone I trust, like Mrs Lund, and having someone sit with me the first few times. I'm not against it, I'm just slow with screens and I don't want to look stupid in front of kids. If I'm forced, I'll learn, but I won't be first.

say: I'd say I'll use AI if it **helps kids learn**, but I won't fake excitement.
I'd tell mates it's like every **new thing** schools buy; the fuss dies down.
think: I think **marking and homework** are what a maths platform does best, and I'm slow at them.
I think struggling with the system becomes another line on my **support plan**.
do: Attend the **platform training** sitting next to Mrs Lund to ask questions.
Let the platform set and mark **Year 7 homework** first, as the lowest risk.
Look into **evening tutoring** rates as a back-up income.
feel: He feels **uneasy and embarrassed** at the thought of another thing to fall behind on.
S1.quote: I'm already behind at the bits I'm meant to be good at. Now there'd be a new thing to be behind on.
fieldNote: He's a **reluctant learner** who'll use AI only once a trusted colleague proves it works.
His fear is specific: a **maths platform** doing his weakest tasks makes him easier to drop.
He is **embarrassed** more than angry, and worries about looking slow in front of pupils.

steps.text: Sit the maths platform training alongside Mrs Lund
Let the platform mark Year 7 homework first
Check evening tutoring rates for GCSE maths as a back-up

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say somebody should slow this down, because schools and parents haven't caught up. At work I'd go quiet, to be honest, and listen to what the head says. I'd probably sign whatever petition the union sends round, even though I'm not a member yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm gone. Maths is the subject a machine does best, and I'm a junior on a support plan who can't use the tools. If they keep any maths teachers, it'll be Mrs Lund and someone like her, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union the same week, because if job cuts are coming I want someone in my corner. I'd ask about being a cover supervisor or a behaviour mentor, which is mostly being a person in a room. And I'd tell Hollie we need to keep every penny, so no holiday and no new car, even when this one dies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly, like the floor's dropped. I spent four years getting into teaching and I'm still not good at it. Two years isn't long enough to get good at anything else either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI comes in 2028 and hands-on robots around 2031. How does that land for a maths teacher?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking part goes first, the explaining, the marking, the planning, and that's nearly all of maths. The hands-on bit, keeping a room calm, standing at the door, comes with robots around 2031. So I might have three years as a cover supervisor, on less money, before even that's up for grabs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Hollie that evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say Hollie's job at the garden centre is the steady one now, which would hurt my pride. We'd probably move in with her mum in the village to stop paying rent. I'd hate that, but Hollie's mum has the space, and she likes me more than my own mum does.

say: I'd say someone should **slow this down** until schools catch up.
I'd go **quiet at work** and sign the union petition even as a non-member.
think: I think **maths** is the subject a machine does best, so I'm gone.
I think any kept teachers will be **experienced** ones like Mrs Lund, not me.
do: Join the **union** the same week to have someone in his corner.
Ask about **cover supervisor** or behaviour mentor posts at Fellside.
Cancel the **holiday** and any car replacement to keep every penny.
feel: He feels **sick**, as if the floor has dropped away.
Two years feels **too short** to get good at anything new.
S2.quote: Maths is the subject a machine does best, and I'm a junior on a support plan who can't use the tools.
fieldNote: He sees maths as the **most exposed** subject and himself as first to go.
The robot gap gives him maybe **three years** as a lower-paid cover supervisor.
He'd **move in** with his girlfriend's mum, swallowing pride to stop paying rent.

steps.text: Join the teachers' union the week the news lands
Apply for cover supervisor or behaviour mentor posts at Fellside
Cancel the summer holiday and keep the old estate car
Move into Hollie's mum's house in the village to stop paying rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still fast and I'd want the government to explain what happens to teachers. At work I'd keep my head down and get off the support plan first. I'd still not post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years mostly means I'd get to the end of my early career just in time for it to end. I'd be thirty-two, a few years in, maybe decent at behaviour by then. But maths as a subject would still be the first thing the AI does better than me in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get off the support plan by summer, that's the first thing. Then I'd use the next couple of years to get a level two coaching badge in football, since I already help with the Year 8 team. And I'd try to put twenty a month away, which isn't much, but it's more than nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grim, more than sick. Five years of warning feels like being told the date of a storm. You can board the windows, but you still lose the roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having five years change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me time to get good at the people part, the behaviour, the coaching, before the robots in 2034. That's the stuff I'd hold on to longest. But I'm not really sure that's a career, or just a slower way out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd only learn the tools if forced. Would five years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes, because by then everyone at Fellside would be using it and I'd look daft not to. I'd ask Mrs Lund to show me in her free period, and practise on the Year 7s. I'd rather learn in my own time than be dragged into it.

say: I'd say it's **still fast** and the government must explain what happens to teachers.
I'd keep my head down at work and get off the **support plan** first.
think: I think I'd reach the end of my early career **just in time** for it to end.
I think **maths** would still be the first thing AI does better than me in 2031.
do: Get off the **support plan** by summer.
Earn a level two **football coaching** badge over the next two years.
Save **twenty a month**, which is more than nothing.
feel: He feels **grim**, like being told the date of a storm.
S3.quote: Five years of warning feels like being told the date of a storm. You can board the windows, but you still lose the roof.
fieldNote: Extra time doesn't ease him much; he still expects **maths teaching** to go in 2031.
He'd use the time on **hands-on skills**: behaviour and football coaching.
He doubts whether those skills are a **career** or just a slower way out.

steps.text: Complete Mr Hale's support plan by the summer term
Earn a level two football coaching badge through the Year 8 team
Save twenty a month from his pay
Practise the maths platform with Mrs Lund in her free period

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if people actually use it. At work I'd say we should plan for it gradually and not let every new app in. I'd still be the one rolling my eyes at the training days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's survivable. I'd be thirty-seven, properly experienced, hopefully good at behaviour, and I could switch to something else if I had to. The worry is that I'm the type who waits too long, and ten years of warning makes it easy to wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd focus on getting good at teaching first, because that's what I need regardless. Over the next few years I'd get the coaching badge and maybe pick up a PE qualification on the side. And I'd learn the maths platform at my own pace once the school buys it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I could sleep. Ten years is a long time in a career, and I'm only at the start. Still, I'd have it in the back of my head every time I marked a test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, where do you see yourself in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe still at Fellside, teaching more PE and less maths, running the football team. Or a head of year, if I've sorted behaviour out by then. Hollie wants to start a family around thirty, so I'd need something steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're in the middle politically. Who do you think should be sorting this out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The government and the exam boards, between them, because they decide what schools teach. Not the tech firms, they'll just sell whatever sells. I don't want handouts, but I'd want help to retrain if it comes to that.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time** if people actually use it.
I'd say schools should plan **gradually** and not let every new app in.
think: I think it's **survivable**, as I'd be thirty-seven and experienced.
I think I'm the type who **waits too long**, and ten years makes waiting easy.
do: Focus on **getting good** at teaching first, which he needs regardless.
Get a **coaching badge** and maybe a PE qualification over the next few years.
Learn the **maths platform** at his own pace once the school buys it.
feel: He feels **uneasy** but could still sleep at night.
The worry would sit in the **back of his head** whenever he marked a test.
S4.quote: I'm the type who waits too long, and ten years of warning makes it easy to wait.
fieldNote: He knows his **resistance** is a risk: a long warning makes waiting tempting.
Plans to start a **family** around thirty raise the stakes on steady pay.
Thin savings and a **remote school** keep him anxious even with a decade.

steps.text: Focus on behaviour management to become a solid maths teacher
Add a PE teaching qualification alongside the coaching badge
Learn the maths platform at his own pace once Fellside buys it

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be gone before I ever got good at the job. What would help is someone actually showing me the tools slowly, and a route into coaching or PE that doesn't need me to stop earning. I'm not asking for a handout, just a ladder.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: How the kids would feel. My Year 11 resit group already think school isn't for them. If a computer can teach maths better than a teacher, those kids will still need someone to tell them they're not thick.

headlineQuote: If a computer can teach maths better than a teacher, those kids will still need someone to tell them they're not thick.
portrait: Gareth is a 27-year-old **maths teacher** at a remote rural secondary, on a support plan for behaviour.
He rents a cold cottage with Hollie, who works at a garden centre, and has **almost no savings**.
He **never uses AI** and will only learn it once a trusted colleague shows him.
He sees maths as **highly exposed**, so fast AGI leaves him alarmed and planning to move in with family.
With a decade he calms slightly but fears his habit of **waiting too long**.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, as he'd be **gone** before he got good at the job.
whatWouldHelp: Someone showing him **AI tools slowly**, in his own time.
A paid route into **coaching or PE** without stopping earning.
